rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Possible events are certain in God's knowledge but doubtful to creatures, so Qur'anic expressions of certainty or hope reflect the relevant perspective.
rows.anchor: والوجه في استعمال هذه الالفاظ أن الامور الممكنة لما كان الخلق يشكون فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knew Pharaoh would not heed the warning, but the wording presents Moses and Aaron's hope that he may take heed.
rows.anchor: وقد علم الله حين ارسلهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic can phrase a certain outcome as doubtful for emphasis: warning that someone may regret an act conveys that regret is inevitable.
rows.anchor: والعرب قد تخرج الكلام المتيقن في صورة المشكوك لاغراض فتقول

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj explains the disbelievers' stated wish to have been Muslims on this same rhetorical principle.
rows.anchor: وبنحو من هذا فسر الزجاج قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's hope of reaching God reflects his ignorance: he wrongly believed that God has a body and occupies a place.
rows.anchor: فاطلاعه إلى الاله مستحيل فبجهله اعتقد

rows.speaker: ابن الدهان
rows.claim: Ibn al-Dahhan allows laʿalla to be used of an impossibility, citing a poem that hopes a bygone age might return.
rows.anchor: ونص ابن الدهان في لعل جواز استعماله في المستحيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whenever God is the subject of ʿasā in the Qur'an, the promised event is certain to occur.
rows.anchor: وقال أيضا كل ما وقع في القرآن من عسى فاعلها الله تعالى فهي واجبة

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some make two exceptions to the rule that divine ʿasā is certain; they cite the prediction that the Prophet might divorce his wives, though he did not.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم إلا في موضعين قال تعالى

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh parses the opening أم as disconnected, equivalent to بل أ, because it follows a declarative statement.
rows.anchor: تقديره بل أيقولون كذا جعلها سيبويه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's question about what people say is phrased from the addressees' perspective, as when Moses and Aaron are told to hope Pharaoh may heed them.
rows.anchor: وقد علم الله أنه لا يتذكر ولا يخشى لكنه اراد لعله يفعل ذلك في رجائكما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here أم means rather and introduces a hamza question of repudiation.
rows.anchor: تقديره بل أتخذ بهمزة منقطعة للإنكار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In another construction, أم can mean بل without an interrogative force.
rows.anchor: وقد تكون بمعنى بل من غير استفهام

rows.speaker: ابن طاهر
rows.claim: Ibn Tahir allows أم meaning بل to function as a coordinating conjunction, citing two examples.
rows.anchor: قال ابن طاهر ( 5 ) ولا يمتنع عندي إذا كانت

rows.speaker: البغوي
rows.claim: Al-Baghawi takes أم as بل here, while most commentators do not regard it as a conjunction.
rows.anchor: وليس بحرف عطف على قول اكثر المفسرين

rows.speaker: الفراء وقوم من أهل المعاني
rows.claim: Al-Farra and some grammarians stop at أم and supply an omitted question before أنا خير; the author says this makes أم disconnected, unlike the alternative connected parsing.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء وقوم من أهل المعاني الوقف على قوله أم

rows.speaker: أبو زيد
rows.claim: Abu Zayd calls أم redundant, supplying the sense: do you not see that I am better than him?
rows.anchor: قال أبو زيد إنها زائدة وإن التقدير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The familiar analysis is disconnected أم: after asserting his claim, Pharaoh doubts that they see and asks whether he is better.
rows.anchor: والمشهور أنها منقطعة لأنه لا يسألهم عن استواء علمه

rows.speaker: ابن طاهر
rows.claim: Ibn Tahir asked his teacher Ibn al-Rammak why Sibawayh did not parse أم as connected; the teacher stayed silent, then resumed teaching after Ibn Tahir reconciled with him.
rows.anchor: وسأل ابن طاهر شيخه أبا القاسم بن الرماك

words: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلْإِنسَٰنُ مَا غَرَّكَ بِرَبِّكَ ٱلْكَرِيمِ
rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view disallows marveling at God's act, since saying how great God is might suggest that something made Him great, whereas His attributes are eternal.
rows.anchor: لايتعجب من فعل الله فلا يقال ما أعظم الله

words: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلْإِنسَٰنُ مَا غَرَّكَ بِرَبِّكَ ٱلْكَرِيمِ
rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view permits such language because magnifying God accords with worshippers' belief in His greatness and power; an anonymous poem says He can bring the distant near.
rows.anchor: وقيل بجوازه باعتبار انه يحب تعظيم الله شيء من صفاته

words: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلْإِنسَٰنُ مَا غَرَّكَ بِرَبِّكَ ٱلْكَرِيمِ
rows.speaker: بعض المحققين
rows.claim: Some scholars answer that astonishment magnifies the matter itself; it need not imply that another agent caused it, and its cause may simply be hidden from us.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض المحققين التعحب انما يقال لتعظيم الامر المتعجب منه

rows.speaker: ابن عصفور
rows.claim: Ibn Asfur prohibits attributing astonishment to God because it entails ignorance, and redirects the apparent expression فما أصبرهم to the human audience.
rows.anchor: وبه جزم ابن عصفور ( 6 ) في المقرب

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Others allow divine astonishment if ما in فما أصبرهم is exclamatory, and cite a reading of بل عجبت with a ḍamma.
rows.anchor: إن قلنا ما تعجبية لا استفهامية

words: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلْإِنسَٰنُ مَا غَرَّكَ بِرَبِّكَ ٱلْكَرِيمِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preferred view treats divine astonishment as directed toward the audience: God knows why people marvel, and His knowledge of what merits wonder is called wonder.
rows.anchor: والمختار الاول وما وقع منه اول بالنظر إلى المخاطب أي علمت اسباب ما يتعجب منه العباد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dispute turns on whether true astonishment requires that the cause of the astonishing matter be hidden.
rows.anchor: وأصل الخلاف في هذه المسالة يلتف على خلاف آخر وهو أن حقيقة التعجب

words: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلْإِنسَٰنُ مَا غَرَّكَ بِرَبِّكَ ٱلْكَرِيمِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'anic exclamation forms are limited to فما أصبرهم على النار, قتل الإنسان ما أكفره, and يا أيها الإنسان ما غرك in a reading that adds a hamza.
rows.anchor: ولم يقع في القرآن صيغة التعجب الا

rows.speaker: المحققون
rows.claim: The learned explain divine exclamation, prayer, and hope from the hearer's perspective; Sibawayh reads 20:44 as Moses and Aaron acting on their own hope, which Ibn al-Da'i praises.
rows.anchor: ثم قال المحققون التعجب مصروف إلى المخاطب ولهذا تلطف الزمخشري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One use of أو is corrective, equivalent to بل, as in descriptions that revise the comparison or number upward.
rows.anchor: الخامس للإضراب ك بل كقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another use of أو is equivalent to واو, including in the paired warning outcomes of 20:44.
rows.anchor: السادس بمعنى الواو كقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In a request, أو may grant permission: either option is allowed, one is sought, and combining them remains permissible; the wording avoids implying that both are required.
rows.anchor: الأول الإباحة نحو تعلم فقها أو نحوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These examples illustrate permissive alternatives: hearts may be likened to stones or harder things, and hypocrites may be represented by either of two parables.
rows.anchor: يعني إن شبهت قلوبهم بالحجارة فصواب أو بما هو أشد فصواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In 20:44, أو permits either of the two outcomes to be sought.
rows.anchor: قوله ﴿ لعله يتذكر أو يخشى ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Choice differs from permission: one alternative must be selected, and combining is impossible, as in the challenge to find a tunnel or ladder.
rows.anchor: الثاني التخيير نحو خذ هذا الثوب أو ذاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammarians classify expiation and pilgrimage ransom alternatives as permission: one satisfies the obligation, combining is allowed, and doing more is better.
rows.anchor: ولهذا مثل النحاة الإباحة بقوله تعالى

rows.speaker: صاحب البسيط
rows.claim: The author reports the Usulists' choice analysis and al-Basit’s reply: combining is forbidden when the unchosen alternative remains prohibited, but extra expiation may be voluntary charity.
rows.anchor: واما تمثيل الأصوليين بآيتي الكفارة والفدية للتخيير مع إمكان الجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ending of al-An'am combines promise and threat, stressing swift punishment while affirming mercy; the passage catalogs how other surah endings suit their themes.
rows.anchor: وكالوعد والوعيد الذى ختمت به سورة الأنعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-A'raf closes by describing the angels and urging worship, while al-Anfal closes with encouragement to jihad and kinship.
rows.anchor: وكالتحريض على العبادة بوصف حال الملائكة الذى ختمت به سورة الأعراف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bara'a's ending describes and honors the Messenger, counts him among the nations, and includes salutations, counsel, and declaration of God's oneness; Yunus and Hud console him.
rows.anchor: ووصف الرسول ومدحه والاعتداد على الأمم به وتسليمه ووصيته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yusuf ends with praise of the Qur'an; al-Ra'd with a response to deniers; Ibrahim with Qur'an praise, its benefit, and God's oneness; al-Hijr with the Prophet's counsel.
rows.anchor: ووصف القرآن ومدحه الذى ختم به سورة يوسف والرد على من كذب الرسول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Nahl closes with consolation and promise, al-Isra with praise, and al-Kahf with a call to deliver the message, proclaim transcendence, and affirm oneness.
rows.anchor: وتسلية الرسول بطمأنينته ووعد الله سبحانه الذى ختمت به النحل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says examples through the first half of the Qur'an can serve as models for examining the remainder.
rows.anchor: وقد أتينا على نصف القرآن ليكون مثالا لمن نظر في بقيته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier surahs recount God destroying peoples and saving their messengers; these surahs focus on the prophets themselves, even when their peoples' fate is not mentioned.
rows.anchor: والسر في ذلك أن تلك السور الأول ذكر الله فيها نصر رسله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Anbiya begins with Abraham because it honors the prophets before Muhammad; Abraham is especially honored, the best of creation, and father to most of them.
rows.anchor: ولهذا سميت سورة الأنبياء فذكر فيها إكرامه للأنبياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although Noah and Lot were not Abraham's descendants, Lot followed him and Job was among his descendants, as al-An'am states.
rows.anchor: وليس هو أب نوح ولوط لكن لوط من أتباعه وأيوب من ذريته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ankabut addresses believers' testing, divine support, and need for striving, and contrasts the good end of the patient with the fate of deniers; Abraham's trial fits this pattern.
rows.anchor: وأما سورة العنكبوت فإنه سبحانه وتعالى ذكر فيها امتحانه للمؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Saffat's warning to observe earlier messengers' outcomes entails a bad end, either defeat and humiliation or destruction.
rows.anchor: وهذا يقتضي أنها عاقبة رديئة إما بكونهم غلبوا وذلوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says Elijah is singled out without mentioning his people's destruction; a report that God raised Elijah implies their punishment is in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: وقد روى أن الله رفع إلياس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elijah, known among the Children of Israel after Moses, did not stay with his people; after Moses, deniers were not annihilated, nor was humanity as a whole after Noah.
rows.anchor: وهذا يقتضي عذابهم في الآخرة فإن إلياس لم يقم بينهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's people are not said to have been destroyed: they cast him into the fire, which God made cool and safe, displaying His proof and humiliating them while supporting Abraham.
rows.anchor: بل ذكر أنهم ألقوه في النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham and Muhammad left their peoples rather than remaining until destruction; they later prevailed. Their success could fulfill the purpose of warning, while some opponents might repent as Jonah's people did.
rows.anchor: وإبراهيم بعد هذا لم يقم بينهم بل هاجر وتركهم وأولئك الرسل لم يزالوا مقيمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an varies Abraham's question about having a son: Aal Imran puts his old age first, while Maryam puts his wife's barrenness first.
rows.anchor: فى آل عمران ﴿ قال رب أنى يكون لي غلام وقد بلغني الكبر وامرأتي عاقر ﴾ وفى كهيعص ﴿ وكانت امرأتي عاقرا وقد بلغت من الكبر عتيا ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ya Sin adds a waw before سواء because its sentence is coordinated with another, whereas al-Baqarah's sentence is the predicate of إن.
rows.anchor: فى البقرة ﴿ سواء عليهم أأنذرتهم أم لم تنذرهم ﴾ وفى يس ﴿ وسواء ﴾ بزيادة واو لأن ما فى البقرة جملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The partitive من in al-Baqarah signals a challenge to the whole Qur'an from its opening onward; omitting it elsewhere avoids making the challenge only to part of a surah.
rows.anchor: لأنها للتبعيض ولما كانت سورة البقرة سنام القرآن وأوله بعد الفاتحة حسن دخول من فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ta-Ha uses اتبع instead of تبع to match its later wording يتبعون الداعي.
rows.anchor: لأجل قوله هناك ﴿ يتبعون الداعي ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Baqarah omits the conjunction before يذبحون, while Ibrahim includes it because Moses is listing the afflictions imposed on the Israelites.
rows.anchor: لأنه من كلام موسى عليه السلام يعدد المحن عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The corresponding clause differs: al-Baqarah includes كانوا, while Aal Imran omits it.
rows.anchor: فى البقرة ﴿ ولكن كانوا أنفسهم يظلمون ﴾ وفى آل عمران ﴿ ولكن أنفسهم يظلمون ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Baqarah first says ومن كان مريضا in the fasting passage, then restates the condition as فمن كان منكم مريضا.
rows.anchor: فى البقرة ﴿ فمن شهد منكم الشهر فليصمه ومن كان مريضا ﴾ ثم قال ﴿ فمن كان منكم مريضا ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This al-Baqarah wording includes من before سيئاتكم, whereas other Qur'anic occurrences omit it.
rows.anchor: وسائر ما فى القرآن بإسقاط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Baqarah omits the threat that God will not look at them, which Aal Imran inserts before ولا يزكيهم.
rows.anchor: وفيها ﴿ ولا يكلمهم الله يوم القيامة ولا يزكيهم ﴾ وفى آل عمران

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only the question about the mountains is answered with فقل; elsewhere answers follow questions, while here the answer precedes the question, as if to say what to answer if asked.
rows.anchor: قالوا وجميع ما فى القرآن من السؤال لم يقع عنه الجواب بالفاء

rows.speaker: المهدوي
rows.claim: Al-Mahdawi reads the dual address in قال قد أجيبت دعوتكما as directed to Moses alone, since he made the supplication.
rows.anchor: وجعل المهدوي منه قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative addresses both Moses and Aaron because Aaron said amen to Moses' prayer and thus shared in supplicating.
rows.anchor: وقيل لهما وكان هارون قد امن على دعائه والمؤمن أحد الداعيين

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says Pharaoh singles Moses out because he bears the great message and distinguished signs.
rows.anchor: أحدهما أنه افرد موسى عليه السلام بالنداء بمعنى التخصيص والتوقف

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari's alternative explanation invokes the Qur'an's statement that Aaron was more eloquent than Moses and the exchange with the challenger.
rows.anchor: ذكره صاحب الكشاف وانظر إلى الفرق بين الجوابين

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya explains the singular فتشقى as addressing Adam, the first person addressed and the main subject of the passage.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية إنما أفرده بالشقاء من حيث كان المخاطب أولا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations say worldly hardship is associated with men, or that the wording courteously leaves the woman unmentioned.
rows.anchor: وقيل بل ذلك لأن الله جعل الشقاء في معيشة الدنيا في حيز الرجال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses and Aaron are described with the singular رسول in their message to Pharaoh.
rows.anchor: وقوله ﴿ فأتيا فرعون فقولا إنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Two addressees can take a plural noun or verb, as in قلوبكما and اختصموا; God also says فتَابَ عليه using one of two for both by implication.
rows.anchor: ونحوه في وصف الاثنين بالجمع

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: When singular address to the Prophet shifts to plural, Ibn al-Anbari says it includes the community with him or honors him by grouping them into his address.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الآنباري إنما جمع في الفعل الثالث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address shifts from Moses and Aaron, to both with their people, then to Moses alone: the leaders receive the first order, the community the worship instruction, and Moses the glad tidings.
rows.anchor: وكذلك قوله ﴿ وأوحينا إلى موسى وأخيه

rows.speaker: الثعلبي
rows.claim: Al-Tha'labi calls this changing form of address al-mutalawwin; scholars of meanings call it iltifat, a topic the author says he will address later.
rows.anchor: وسماه الثعلبي المتلون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sky and earth answer in the masculine plural طائعين, though a feminine dual might be expected, because they are represented as speaking rational beings.
rows.anchor: الثاني والعشرون خطاب الجمادات خطاب من يعقل

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: The two explanations are literal speech after God gave the bodies life and perception, or figurative speech for their manifested willing submission; Ibn Atiyya prefers literal speech because nothing rules it out and it better displays divine power.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية والآول أحسن لأنه لاشيء يدفعه والعبرة فيه أتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mountains are commanded with the feminine singular form used for addressing inanimate things.
rows.anchor: لأن جميع مالا يعقل كذلك يؤمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Conditional challenges such as if you are believers exhort people to trust, fear God, leave usury, obey, or rely on Him; they do not deny the faith of anyone who falls short.
rows.anchor: ولايدل على ان من لم يتوكل ينتفي عنهم الايمان بل حث لهم على التوكل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These conditional phrases exhort believers to act consistently with faith; this is better than interpreting إن as إذ.
rows.anchor: وهذا احسن من قول من قال إن هاهنا بمعنى إذ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition against befriending those who fought and expelled the believers exemplifies address intended to provoke anger.
rows.anchor: الرابع والعشرون خطاب الإغضاب كقوله تعالى

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: When wording requires two things but mentions one, Ibn Atiyya says Pharaoh says only Moses because he is the main bearer of the message.
rows.anchor: لأن موسى المقصود المتحمل أعباء الرسالة كذا قاله ابن عطية

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says Pharaoh began to add Aaron's name but refrained, wary of Aaron's eloquence and sharp reply.
rows.anchor: وغاص الزمخشري فقال أراد أن يتم الكلام فيقول وهارون

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari expands the omitted sense: they disperse toward trade or toward amusement, with the second pronoun understood from the first.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري تقديره إذا رأوا تجارة انفضوا إليها

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib explains why the pronoun refers to trade: it caused the dispersal, and trade can distract from worship more than amusement.
rows.anchor: قال الراغب في تفسير سورة البقرة إن التجارة لما كانت سبب انفضاض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in ولا ينفقونها can refer to silver, the nearer and more common, needed, and frequently hoarded metal; another view takes it as the collective sense of hoarded wealth.
rows.anchor: أعاد الضمير على الفضة وحدها لأنها أقرب المذكورين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural verb اقتتلوا after the dual طائفتان reflects that each طائفة is a group.
rows.anchor: لأن الطائفة جماعة وقيل من عادة العرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic can mention two semantically related nouns but agree the verb or pronoun with only one, relying on the listener to understand the shared sense; Hassan's verse uses singular يعاص.
rows.anchor: وقيل من عادة العرب إذا ذكرت شيئين مشتركين في المعنى تكتفي بإعادة الضمير على أحدهما

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari takes the pronoun in لم تروها to refer to the unseen troops rather than the wind.
rows.anchor: وقد جعل ابن لأنباري في كتاب الهاءات 4 ضمير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author lists shifts from third-person reference to first-person plural, including the night journey, ordering the heavens, the claim that God has a child, and cloud movement.
rows.anchor: من الغيبة إلى التكلم كقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: First-person wording for driving clouds toward a land marks revival through rain as a striking sign of power unique to God, heightening exclusivity and grandeur.
rows.anchor: وفائدته أنه لما كان سوق السحاب إلى البلد إحياء للأرض بعد موتها بالمطر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majestic plural can signal agents acting under God's command: winds drive clouds and angels move them, while Gabriel recites and God gathers the guilty; rain revives earth through ordained causes.
rows.anchor: فتسوقه الملائكة بأمره وإحياء الأرض به بواسطة إنزاله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sending the clouds is described without an intermediary cause, unlike driving them and sending rain, whose causes are stated.
rows.anchor: وأما إرسال السحاب فهو سحاب يأذن في إرسالها ولم يذكر له سببا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author cites other rain and planting passages as examples of first-person divine action after causes are described.
rows.anchor: بخلاف سوق السحاب وإنزال المطر فإنه قد ذكر أسبابه

words: وَأَنزَلَ مِنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ مَآءًۭ فَأَخْرَجْنَا بِهِۦٓ أَزْوَٰجًۭا مِّن نَّبَاتٍۢ شَتَّىٰ
rows.speaker: الجرجاني
rows.claim: Al-Jurjani calls the Ta-Ha passage an iltifat, taking Moses' speech to end at وأنزل من السماء ماء and God's first-person report to begin at فأخرجنا.
rows.anchor: وزعم الجرجاني أن في هذه الآية التفاتا

words: فَأَخْرَجْنَا بِهِۦٓ أَزْوَٰجًۭا مِّن نَّبَاتٍۢ شَتَّىٰ
rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says first-person shifts draw attention to God's exclusive power; another explanation says they vividly present scenes of distinctive or striking acts.
rows.anchor: وأشار الزمخشري 6 إلى أن فائدة الالتفات إلى التكلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording تصبح الأرض مخضرة indicates that the rain continues over time.
rows.anchor: لإفادة بقاء المطر زمانا بعد زمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The default order places subject before object, topic before predicate, and possessor before its circumstantial phrase unless a reason favors change.
rows.anchor: أحدها أن يكون أصله التقديم ولا مقتضى للعدول عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Placing من آل فرعون before يكتم إيمانه makes clear that the believing man belongs to Pharaoh's people; delaying it would obscure that meaning.
rows.anchor: فإنه لو أخر قوله ﴿ من آل فرعون ﴾ فلا يفهم أنه منهم

rows.speaker: السكاكي
rows.claim: Al-Sakkaki says من قومه is advanced before الذين كفروا to prevent the phrase seeming to describe worldly life; another verse safely delays it because the ambiguity is absent.
rows.anchor: وجعل السكاكي 2 من الأسباب كون التأخير مانعا

words: وَٱسْجُدُوا۟ لِلَّهِ ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَهُنَّ إِن كُنتُمْ إِيَّاهُ تَعْبُدُونَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Putting إياه before تعبدون preserves the cadence and sound pattern of the verse endings.
rows.anchor: الثالث أن يكون في التأخير إخلال بالتناسب فيقدم 4 لمشاكلة الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The placement in فأوجس في نفسه خيفة موسى maintains the sequence of verse endings around it.
rows.anchor: فات تناسب الفواصل لأن قبله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The subject النار is delayed after the object وجوههم to harmonize with what follows.
rows.anchor: فإن تأخير الفاعل عن المفعول لمناسبته لما بعده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ending إن الله سريع الحساب is chosen because it fits the preceding image of the condemned bound in fetters.
rows.anchor: وهو أشكل بما قبله لأن قبله

rows.speaker: السكاكي
rows.claim: Al-Sakkaki treats Aaron's mention before Moses as an order chosen for cadence, although Moses has the stronger claim to precedence.
rows.anchor: وجعل منه السكاكي 1 ﴿ آمنا برب هارون وموسى
